cohorts.label: 20-100h
cohorts.summary: Players face punishing economic and army challenges, though community mods expand the experience.

claims.claim: Reviewers report that community-created mods on the Steam Workshop significantly enhance or carry the gameplay experience.

citations.review_text: One of the best games ever. Don't forget to mod it after you get a hang of the game.

An engaging sandbox game where you can build your own army and kingdom, battle feudal lords, conquer territories, and lay siege to fortresses and cities. Build your empire and clear the entire continent of enemies. A huge selection of mods to suit every taste: from ancient times to ‘Star Wars’ and magical worlds. The fields are littered with hundreds of corpses, with battles involving up to ~150 units at once. A wide variety of weapons. Intrigues between lords and subjects of the kingdoms, marriages, and much more. Still relevant today. Don your plate armour, master the use of two-handed weapons, and smash your enemies’ heads in!

Personally, I find every part of this game that isn't the battles mind-numbingly boring. However, there hasn't been a game since that's improved on the large-scale battles you can gawk at like Mount and Blade. The Steam Workshop contains a metric ass-load of mods that provide much more enriching experiences than vanilla Mount and Blade. Personally, I would recommend the Diplomacy mod.

Raising your army, losing soldiers, recruiting and training new ones, and then losing them, while struggling to sustain them in the awful economy, is part of the experience. It is worth trying if you are into medieval times, unintentionally old but gold graphics, and army management. This game has a good modding community, too.

I Came for the Castle, I Stayed for the Addiction
Mount & Blade: Warband is one of those games where you start as a nobody and somehow end up telling people about the time you defended a castle against an army five times your size.

I still remember walking through a castle for the first time and seeing NPCs moving around. It sounds simple now, but back then it felt like I had stepped into a real world.

Then came the battles, the companions, the betrayals, the terrible decisions, and the moments where you think: "There is no way I win this." Then somehow you do.

One day you’re a Swadian Knight charging into battle. Another day you’re a Rhodok Sharpshooter holding a castle wall. Then mods happen and suddenly you’re a Noldor-loving archer in Pendor, a samurai in Gekokujo, a Wood Elf in Warsword, or a vampire necromancer with guns.

The graphics are old, the AI can be questionable, and your companions will definitely complain about something. But somehow, hundreds of hours later, you’re still here.

Warband isn’t perfect. It’s better.

It’s a game where you don’t just complete a story—you accidentally create one.

10/10. Would lose another save file again.

Perhaps the single best video game ever made. Oh how nostalgic I am of playing NW line battles, NA duel for hours and the many multiplayer mods. Let alone all the amazing single player experiences from Native to Viking conquest and Pendor.
One of the best medieval sandbox games ever. And if you want something different, the mods can turn it into a completely new game.

This game is old but it is one-of-kind. The vanilla game is very fun and rewarding to play and once you have gotten enough of that, there are lots of complete overhaul mods to push this game to be better, overall, than its' sequel Bannerlord. 

Also since this game is pretty old, it can be run on basically any modern computer without issue. Furthermore, there is the Warband Script Enhancer 2 which can improve performance even more, making even the largest intensive overhaul mods available load in seconds.

Even after all these years, Mount & Blade: Warband is still one of the most unique games I've ever played.

It doesn't rely on flashy graphics or cinematic storytelling. Instead, it gives you complete freedom. You can become a mercenary, a trader, a bandit, a loyal vassal, or build your own kingdom from nothing. Every playthrough creates its own story.

The combat feels simple at first, but mastering directional attacks, blocking, horseback fighting, and commanding your troops is incredibly satisfying. Large battles are chaotic in the best way, and winning through good tactics feels rewarding.

What really keeps this game alive is the modding community. There are hundreds of amazing mods that can completely transform the game, adding new worlds, historical settings, fantasy overhauls, and countless hours of extra content.

Warband definitely shows its age, and some mechanics can feel clunky compared to modern games. But if you're looking for a sandbox RPG where your decisions actually shape your adventure, it's still one of the best games you can buy.

It's easy to sink hundreds—or even thousands—of hours into this game.

Highly recommended.
